subject: pathology
title: Hypersensitivity reactions and transplant rejection

steps.tx: Hypersensitivity is an exaggerated or misdirected immune response that injures the host. Gell and Coombs classify it into four types. Type I is **IgE-mediated** and immediate. Antigen cross-links IgE bound to sensitised **mast cells** and basophils, releasing histamine and other vasoactive amines. Examples include anaphylaxis, asthma, urticaria and the wheal and flare reaction. Type I reactions appear within minutes of exposure.

steps.tx: Type II is **antibody-mediated cytotoxicity**. IgG or IgM binds an antigen on a host cell, which is then destroyed by complement or phagocytosis. Examples include autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ITP and myasthenia gravis. In **Goodpasture syndrome**, antibodies target type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. The result is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary haemorrhage, and linear IgG deposition is seen on immunofluorescence.
steps.say: Type two is antibody mediated cytotoxicity. IgG or IgM binds an antigen on a host cell, which is then destroyed by complement or phagocytosis. Examples include autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ITP and myasthenia gravis. In Goodpasture syndrome, antibodies target type four collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. The result is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with pulmonary haemorrhage, and linear IgG deposition is seen on immunofluorescence.

steps.tx: Type III is **immune complex mediated**. Complexes deposit in vessel walls or membranes, fix complement and attract neutrophils. Examples include SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, PSGN and polyarteritis nodosa. **Serum sickness** appears about 5 to 10 days after exposure, with fever, urticaria, arthralgia, proteinuria and lymphadenopathy. Most cases now follow drugs rather than animal serum. The **Arthus reaction** is a local type III reaction. Intradermal antigen meets preformed antibody, producing oedema, haemorrhage and necrosis within 4 to 10 hours.

steps.tx: Type IV is **T-cell mediated** and delayed. It takes 12 to 48 hours because effector T cells must be recruited. Sensitised CD4 TH1 cells release cytokines that activate macrophages. Repeated stimulation can form **granulomas**, made of epithelioid cells with a lymphocyte collar. Examples include the tuberculin test, contact dermatitis, granulomatous disease and graft rejection. Because it is cell mediated, it cannot be transferred by serum. Contact dermatitis from urushiol is a classic exam example.

Examples include the tuberculin test, contact dermatitis, granulomatous disease and graft rejection. Because it is cell mediated, it cannot be transferred by serum. steps.tx: Transplant rejection follows timing. **Hyperacute** rejection happens within minutes to hours. Preformed anti-donor antibodies, often anti-HLA or ABO, cause thrombosis and ischaemic necrosis. It is now rare because of crossmatching, and no immunosuppression helps. **Acute cellular** rejection occurs days to weeks later and is the most common type. T cells attack foreign MHC, giving mononuclear infiltration, usually reversible with immunosuppression. **Chronic** rejection occurs over months to years, with intimal fibrosis and graft atrophy, and is difficult to treat.

steps.tx: **Graft versus host disease** occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells attack an immunosuppressed recipient. It is seen mainly after haematopoietic stem cell transplant. Acute GVHD, within about 100 days, classically causes a skin rash, bloody diarrhoea and jaundice. Chronic GVHD, after 100 days, causes skin fibrosis and oesophageal stricture. Prevention relies on HLA matching. Remember the donor T cell is the culprit, not the host.
